description: We are a brother duo built on a strong STEM foundation. One of us brings a background in biophysics and interdisciplinary science, while the other combines a sharp eye for detail with creative computer science, logic, and data analysis. Grounded in our STEM education, we both share a passion for breaking down complex systems from the ground up, working with numbers, and tackling technical challenges together.
summary: Muscle loss during long space missions varies across muscle groups, making early deterioration difficult to identify from isolated measurements. MuscleMap is an offline-ready tool that helps astronauts track regional muscle health, interpret changes, and decide when to repeat a scan or seek medical review. We'll build an interactive muscle map, longitudinal trend analysis, and quality-aware, explainable alerts. NASA's CFT70 bed-rest research and in-flight ultrasound studies will guide the model and validation, with clearly labeled simulated readings for the prototype.
details:
We started MuscleMap with a question: how can astronauts actually understand what is happening to their muscles throughout a space mission, rather than just looking at separate measurements and trying to make sense of them?

Muscle loss is a known problem in microgravity, and astronauts already follow exercise programs to reduce its effects. But muscle size, physical performance, and exercise activity don't necessarily tell the same story. They're measured differently, at different times, and interpreting them together isn't always straightforward.

MuscleMap is our attempt to make that process easier. It's a web-based musculoskeletal monitoring system built around an interactive 3D anatomical model. Users can select a measured muscle region, explore how its measurements have changed relative to a personal baseline, and understand what the available evidence actually supports. The application also allows users to import or manually record new observations, document follow-ups, and export reports that preserve the original measurements and their sources.

We built the research demonstration using four NASA CFT70 ultrasound and MRI datasets from a 70-day bed-rest study involving 27 participants. These are ground-based research measurements, not actual astronaut records. We use them to demonstrate longitudinal monitoring while keeping the limitations of the data visible.

Technically, we developed MuscleMap using TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, and Python for data preparation, with local storage and offline support. We also included an Incident Support feature for documenting sudden muscular concerns and organizing information for medical handover.

What makes MuscleMap different, in our view, isn't simply the 3D anatomy or the graphs. It's the way the application handles the evidence behind them. We deliberately avoided inventing measurements, treating unrelated data as interchangeable, or producing medical conclusions that the available data couldn't support.

Our goal is to make muscular health monitoring more understandable and useful for astronauts, particularly during missions where medical support from Earth may not always be immediately available. MuscleMap isn't meant to replace medical professionals, but to help astronauts recognize changes, understand uncertainty, and approach follow-up decisions with clearer information.
